title: Spill oscillation thresholds and bank coupling — lab digest
content:
Summary:

This is a working lab digest from a sequence of microbenchmarks and multi-hour workload runs exploring a phenomenon we've been calling "spill oscillation": periodic cycles where pages/entries are spilled to NVMe, then re-paged back shortly after, causing bandwidth storms and tail latency spikes. Focus is on how eviction thresholds and bank-aware pacing interact (i.e., bank coupling), and where the sweet spot is between tail latency and total token cost.

Key takeaways (short):
- A conservative high-residency threshold (~88–92% occupancy) reduces NVMe I/O but exposes long-tail latency during hot-window surges.
- Aggressive eviction (threshold <70%) stabilizes tail latency but increases NVMe write amplification and end-to-end cost ~7–12% for this workload mix.
- Bank-coupled pacing (spread evictions across memory banks and stagger prefetch) reduced instantaneous DDR bandwidth peaks by ~25% and mitigated the worst of the oscillation.
- Prefetch delays (30–50ms tunable delay) combined with bank pacing smooth re-access patterns and reduced re-touch rate from 14%->6% in the dataset.

Background and hypothesis:
We observe recurring tails in production when multi-tenant chat workloads hit short hot streaks (many requests reusing similar KV pages). Hypothesis: eviction and immediate prefetch/restore interplay creates a feedback loop: eviction -> request hits -> synchronous page-in -> eviction of other pages -> more misses -> NVMe flood -> latencies spike, causing more requests to queue -> worsened tail. Bank-level memory contention amplifies this: simultaneous dma reads across a couple of memory channels cause momentary BW saturation and PCIe queueing.

Experiment environment (brief):
- cluster: staging-serving-64 (8xA100-80G per node used in dedicated tests)
- runtime: serving-runtime@main (commit f9a3b6), profiling-enabled build
- nvme: 2x1.6TB NVMe per node (Samsung PM1733)
- kernel: Ubuntu 22.04 + custom io_uring tweaks for async page fetch
- measurement: perf counters, nvmetop, /proc/vmstat, and a tracing hook that emits per-request (reuse_count, eviction_count, page_faults)
- workload: mixed chat: 60% short convs (seqlen 32–96), 40% long prompts (seqlen 512–2048). Synthetic hot-key injection used to vary hot-window properties.

Test matrix (representative runs):
- Baseline: eviction_threshold=80%, bank_pacing=off, prefetch_delay=0ms
- Run A: threshold=92%, bank_pacing=off, prefetch_delay=0ms
- Run B: threshold=70%, bank_pacing=off, prefetch_delay=0ms
- Run C: threshold=80%, bank_pacing=enabled (spread=4ms stagger per bank), prefetch_delay=0ms
- Run D: threshold=80%, bank_pacing=enabled, prefetch_delay=40ms
- Long-run: 6hr run with Run D params and hotshot injections every 15 minutes to validate stability

Raw observations (selected):
- Baseline:
  - median latency (inference + IO): 52ms
  - p95: 240ms, p99: 1.4s
  - NVMe writes: 2.1 GB/hr
  - reuse_rate overall: 62% (re-use of existing KV entries without page-in)
  - re-touch rate (pages spilled then repaged within 1s): 14%

- Run A (high residency 92%):
  - median: 50ms; p95: 210ms; p99: 2.1s (tail worsened)
  - NVMe writes: 0.9 GB/hr (drops ~57%)
  - reuse_rate: 72% (expected)
  - re-touch rate: 18% (slightly higher)

- Run B (aggressive eviction 70%):
  - median: 60ms; p95: 190ms; p99: 600ms (tails improved)
  - NVMe writes: 2.8 GB/hr (write amplification +33%)
  - reuse_rate: 51%
  - re-touch rate: 12%

- Run C (bank pacing enabled):
  - median: 55ms; p95: 200ms; p99: 850ms
  - NVMe writes: 1.9 GB/hr
  - peak DDR BW reduced by 25% (measured via imc counters)
  - occurrences of spike cycles ( >1s tails) down from 7/hr -> 3/hr

- Run D (pacing + prefetch delay 40ms):
  - median: 53ms; p95: 195ms; p99: 720ms
  - NVMe writes: 1.6 GB/hr
  - re-touch rate: 6% (big win)
  - tail spike cycles: 1/hr in 6hr long-run stability test

Notes on measurements and noise model:
- We instrumented per-request KV metrics: entry_found, page_fault_sync_time, async_page_issue_time, and eviction_tag. Correlated page_fault_sync_time spikes align almost exactly with DDR BW peaks and NVMe IO queue depth increases.
- There is nontrivial jitter from tenant co-location. We attempted to stabilize by pinning tests to single tenant slices; results above aggregate multi-tenant runs with controlled background noise.
- PCIe controller queue depth occasionally showed blocking at NVMe driver level during raw floods; adding a jitter to prefetch reduced synchronous driver stalls.

Interpretation / root cause sketch:
- When eviction is too conservative, we keep more pages resident which sounds good for reuse, but when the hot-window shifts the system ends up with a burst of pages that were never warmed (cold portions of the resident set). Subsequent re-warming produces synchronous page_ins that align and saturate memory channels.
- Aggressive eviction decreases the size of the resident set and therefore reduces probability of those synchronized re-warms, but increasing NVMe churn (higher writes) and higher steady-state cost.
- Bank-aware pacing splits eviction and prefetch work across memory channels, which lowers instantaneous bandwidth demand and avoids driver/PCIe bottlenecks. Prefetch delay allows opportunity for duplicate requests to be coalesced or for small transient surges to pass without forcing a prefetch.

Actionable recommendations (short term):
1) Add bank-pacing as a configurable default for dedicated clusters with these NVMe characteristics. Start with stagger=4ms per bank and tune. (PR: see linked PR #4123)
2) Introduce an adaptive prefetch delay: start from 40ms and decay to 5ms if re-touch rate falls below 5% over a 2-min window. Rationale: avoids unnecessary prefetches for short transient surges.
3) Telemetry: emit a new metric kv_retouch_rate_{1s,5s} and eviction_bank_spread to monitor oscillation in prod.
4) Cost-mode: for cost-sensitive customers expose an "aggressive-eviction" knob (threshold <=72%) with warnings about increased NVMe usage.

Open questions / next experiments:
- How does this interact with quantized model paths where KV storage per token is reduced? Hypothesis: quantized models reduce NVMe churn proportional to KV size but similar oscillation patterns persist. Need to run mixed-quantization trials.
- Is there benefit to changing eviction selection policy to preferentially pick victims in banks that already show high residency, i.e., bias eviction toward overfull banks? Could reduce re-touch locality.
- Explore a multi-level prefetch that does lazy async read (no blocking) then optional sync fallback after X ms. We only tested static delays so far.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Carlos: can you add perf event capture around PCIe queue depth for the long-run next week? (ticket SERVE-987)
- Amina: prototype bank_pacing toggle in staging (PR draft in #4123). Leave it off by default until telemetry validated.
- Ethan: simulate smaller model KV footprints (8-bit quantized) and repeat Run D. Estimate NVMe delta.

Links and references:
- design doc sketch: confluence://design/kv-bank-throttling
- PR with bank_pacing prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/4123
- Jira for tracking follow-ups: https://jira.redwood.ai/browse/SERVE-987

Appendix (commands / short snippets used):
- per-request trace capture (local replay): bin/trace_capture --trace-kv --out /tmp/trace.json
- perf counters snippet used: sudo perf stat -e mem-loads,mem-stores,LLC-load-misses -I 1000 -p <pid>
- nvme monitoring: sudo watch -n1 nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0n1; nvme top (custom)

Bottom line: bank-aware pacing + small prefetch delay is the most promising immediate mitigation for production oscillations. It provides a practical middle ground between steady-state cost and tail-latency stability. We'll iterate on adaptive delay and targeted eviction heuristics next quarter.

(End of digest — feedback welcome; this is intentionally rough notes rather than a formal postmortem.)
